title: Labbook: bridge-mode PCIe vs NVLink comparison (A100/H100/L40S)
content:
Purpose:
This labbook captures an exploratory set of experiments comparing bridge-mode (NVLink-enabled multi-GPU fabric) vs plain PCIe interconnect behavior for our serving runtime across three representative cloud GPU families: NVIDIA A100, H100, and L40S. The goal is to isolate how interconnect topology and driver/PCIe link state impact tail latency, jitter, and decode throughput for both short-context and long-context inference workloads.

Scope and motivation (quick):
- We suspect some p99 tail amplification events correlate to inter-GPU fabric state transitions (link training / throttling) when requests span multiple devices or when KV-cache rehydration touches remote memory.
- Customers running multi-GPU model sharding or per-request routing to different GPUs see inconsistent tails across regions and instance types.
- This notebook is intentionally exploratory: multiple knobs, lots of telemetry, loose hypotheses. Later we can distill a smaller set of regression tests.

High-level hypotheses (to test):
1) NVLink/bridge-mode reduces average cross-GPU prefill latency but may amplify rare long tails when link flaps or power/cooling governor events occur.
2) PCIe-only instances show higher median latency under small-batch steady-state but fewer extreme tails when NVLink driver versions mismatch.
3) H100 exhibits different sensitivity to CUDA/driver combos than A100 due to different link management and power states; L40S behaves closer to A100 for short decode but differs on sustained throughput.

Test matrix (planned):
- GPUs: A100 40GB/80GB (single-socket multi-GPU), H100 80GB, L40S 48GB (public cloud SKUs selected below).
- Cloud SKUs (examples): AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100 + NVLink), GCP a2-megagpu/ultra (A100/40GB variants), Azure NDm_A100_v4, AWS h1g? (H100 equivalents: in practice use AWS p5 variants), GCP L40S SKUs where available. (Note: exact SKU naming differs by cloud/region; use nearest available when scheduling).
- Interconnect modes: bridge-mode/NVLink (where platform exposes it) vs PCIe-only (e.g., instances with NVLink disabled or MIG partitions with NVSwitch isolated).
- Driver/CUDA versions: primary matrix: CUDA 11.8 / 11.7 / 12.1; NVIDIA driver versions tested: 525.x, 535.x, 550.x (pick platform-supported combos).
- Workloads: small-batch low-latency chat path (prefill=128 tokens, decode=1 token streaming, batch=1-4) and long-context generation (prefill=8192 tokens, decode=1024, batch=1, sustained). Also a mixed burst pattern (bursts of 16 concurrent small requests).
- KV cache patterns: cold start (no KV), warm with local KV, warm with remote KV (simulated by forcing cross-GPU remote reads).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latencies, tail clusters (time-of-day/host correlation), jitter (stddev of per-token latency), throughput (tokens/sec), memory HW counters (NVLink retries, PCIe replay counts if available), GPU clocks/power, CPU offload time, kernel launch rates.

Test harness notes (implementation details):
- Use the same runtime binary build for all runs (branch: perf/bridge-probe-2025) with debug logging options to toggle detailed telemetry.
- Sampling: run 3 independent runs per configuration, each 30 minutes steady-state after 5-minute warmup. For long-context runs we perform 3 x 60m runs.
- Telemetry collectors: nvidia-smi telemetry for power/clock; nvlink stats via NVML metrics where possible; eBPF traces on kernel to capture PCIe device resets or AER (if permitted by cloud); runtime-level traces (per-request timestamps, kernel launch timestamps).
- Time sync: ensure chrony/ntp consistent across VMs; annotate runs with host-level load and background noisy neighbors.

Preliminary findings (notes from first two sweep days):
- A100 (NVLink enabled): median prefill latency improved ~8-12% compared to PCIe-only when cross-GPU KV reads were required. However we observed occasional p999 spikes (3–4x baseline) that correlated with NVLink retries counter increments on the host. These spikes happened more frequently on older driver versions (525.x).
- H100: median showed smaller gains from NVLink vs PCIe (2–5%) but tails were much more sensitive to driver version. On CUDA 12.1 + driver 550.x, p99 stabilized; on older drivers p99 moved up 30–50% for the same workload.
- L40S: behaved like A100 for prefill but under sustained decode throughput across long contexts, L40S lost ~8% tokens/sec compared to H100 when NVLink used for remote KV. L40S NVLink telemetry visibility is more limited on some clouds, making attribution harder.
- PCIe-only: Lower variance in tails during bursts in general, but higher median latency for tests that required remote memory access (makes sense).

Concrete examples (from run logs):
- Run: a100-ptx-2x (NVLink), CUDA 11.8, driver 525.89:
  - small-batch chat: p50 18ms, p95 42ms, p99 120ms, p999 490ms (three p999 events observed). NVLink retry counter increased by 3 at timestamps matching p999s.
- Run: h100-svc-1 (NVLink), CUDA 12.1, driver 550.30:
  - long-context sustained: tokens/sec 19.6k, p99 210ms; older driver 535.86 same workload: tokens/sec 18.1k, p99 320ms.

Open hypotheses after initial sweep:
- Driver/firmware interplay: older drivers trigger link-level retransmits under heavy kernel launch fanout. Upgrading driver reduces retransmit counts and tail events.
- Power/thermal governor interactions: NVLink-nav changes when GPUs enter lower power states under low utilization, causing transient renegotiation events. Need to correlate with clock throttling logs.
- PCIe replay/AER events: when present, they line up with very large spikes; cloud providers sometimes hide these events so runs must be cross-checked with host telemetry.

Short checklist for reproducibility before wider run: (TODOs)
- [ ] Standardize instance selection across clouds (map equivalence table and list of regions).
- [ ] Add automated script to toggle NVLink/bridge mode where cloud exposes it, and capture nvlink counters pre/post test.
- [ ] Instrument runtime to emit per-request device-local vs device-remote KV read flag.
- [ ] Add eBPF probe to capture PCIe resets/AER on hosts (coordinate with cloud support to avoid policy violations).
- [ ] Formalize driver matrix and lock a couple of driver+cuda combos as golden.

Immediate next experiments (week plan):
1) Driver sweep on H100 across 535.x, 550.x while running sustained 8k-context job; capture retry counts and clock transitions.
2) Small-batch burst test on A100 comparing NVLink vs PCIe across two different AZs to check if host placement affects link stability.
3) Inject controlled background NVLink noise (where permitted) by running synthetic DMA stress to see if it reproduces p999s.

Questions / open items for team:
- Can SRE procure instances with explicit NVLink disable/enable control in our accounts? Some clouds require support requests. (ask: Gareth)
- Is there existing infra to collect NVLINK-level counters centrally? We currently push nvidia-smi samples to metrics but NVML NVLINK specific fields are not scraped. (ask: Observability team)
- Are we allowed to run eBPF PCIe probes on managed instances? We need policy/approval. (ask: infra/ops)

Notes-to-self (rough):
- When seeing a p999 spike, always check three sources: NVML nvlink.* metrics, kernel dmesg for AER/PCIe errors, runtime trace for long syscall or CPU offload.
- Keep a copy of the exact AMI/image/container hash in run metadata.
- Beware auto-driver updates on image rollouts; pin driver in test image.

Suggested artifact outputs from this project:
- Compact bench report (1–2 pages) summarizing delta between NVLink vs PCIe across GPUs and drivers.
- A small synthetic test (open-source) that reproduces the NVLink retry-induced tail under controlled conditions (helpful for cloud provider tickets).
- A nightly Canary run (reduced sample) that checks p99 regression on a locked driver+cuda combo.

Appendix: quick checklist for running a single configuration manually
1) Launch instance(s) with requested SKU and region.
2) Pull image: ghcr.io/redwood/serving-runtime:perf-bridge-2025-rc1 and note image hash.
3) Ensure driver installed (exact version) and record nvml/nvidia-smi output.
4) Start runtime with --telemetry nvlink,pcie,kernel-launch; attach log stream to perf-collector.
5) Warmup 5m, then run steady test for target duration.
6) Save raw traces, nvml dumps, and host dmesg to s3://redwood-perf-lab/bridge-mode/<run-id>.tar.gz

Contact: Maya Chen (owner) — ping in #eng-serving-runtime with subject "bridge-mode labbook" for quick sync.

End of labbook entry (draft). Will iterate into a condensed summary + slide with top-line numbers after the driver sweep completes.
